items.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003
items.q: the bass like Ray Brown or Paul Chambers or Richard Davis or any — Charlie Mingus. You know? I have learned how to be Larry Ridley. Because — as the Bible says, to thine own self be true. Of course I’ve learned from them and there are certain things that I have picked up from them

ctx.x: The group with Freddie Hubbard and Jimmy Spaulding and first Walt Miller then Al Plank and Paul Parker was the drummer. And then we used to play with Wes. The first time I saw Monk Montgomery and I approached him about taking lessons from him he told me, “Well come over to the house, kid.” I went over to the house and there is Wes sitting up there with the guitar and his brother Buddy at the piano. A saxophone player by the name of Pookie Johnson and the drummer Sonny Johnson. They called themselves the…

having good ears. You know because when you’re up there improvising you’re not thinking about oh I’m going from a D minor seventh with a flat five over here to a G seven with a raised nine. You’re not thinking about all that. You’ve got to sit at the piano and you’ve got to get that sound, or the guitar, and get those sounds in your ear and know how to respond to that improvisationally through hearing lyrical lines. And that’s one of the things I’m concerned about that is happening with jazz education. Too many…
How can you foster that ability to invent melodies and what happened to you with this — being thrown in that situation? How can we do that now?
